content.text:
Yes, but two things have to be solved first, and neither is a blocker you'd hit with an ordinary GUI app.

**Where things stand:** `gcloud` is installed here and authenticated as the `ai-agent@tsdtechnology.iam.gserviceaccount.com` service account (project `elegoo-backend`), so I can create and drive a Windows VM without your involvement. What I can't do is see a Windows desktop the way you would — I have no RDP client wired into my tools, and my screenshot tool only captures your Mac's screen.

**Problem 1 — OpenGL.** This is the real one, and it's specific to this app. OrcaSlicer refuses to start when OpenGL is below 3.2 — [OpenGLManager.cpp:288](src/slic3r/GUI/OpenGLManager.cpp:288) pops "The application cannot run normally because OpenGL version is lower than 3.2" and quits. A stock GCE Windows VM has no GPU, and Windows' built-in software renderer reports OpenGL 1.1, so the app would die at launch. Two ways around it:

- Drop a Mesa3D software `opengl32.dll` (the llvmpipe build) next to the .exe. That reports OpenGL 4.5 and runs entirely on CPU — no GPU, no license, works on the cheapest VM. Slow 3D view, fine for UI and layout verification. This is my recommendation.
- Attach an NVIDIA GPU with the virtual-workstation driver. Real hardware OpenGL, but more cost, more setup, and the vWS licensing wrinkle.

**Problem 2 — somebody has to be logged in.** On Windows, a GUI app launched from a non-interactive remote shell runs in a session with no visible desktop, so a screenshot comes back black. The fix is standard: enable auto-logon so the console session is always live, then run the app and the screen-capture script inside that session as a scheduled task. I'd capture PNGs server-side with PowerShell, pull them down with `gcloud compute scp`, and look at them here. Clicking would be scripted (PowerShell/AutoHotkey sending input into the session) rather than me pointing at pixels.

**One shortcut worth considering:** you already have Windows CI. `.github/workflows/build_orca.yml` builds Windows, so I'd pull an artifact instead of setting up Visual Studio and building deps on the VM — that alone saves hours per iteration.

**The other option**, if you want me driving a real interactive desktop: install Microsoft Remote Desktop on your Mac, connect to the VM, and I use the computer-use tools to see and click inside that window. That gets me a genuine interactive session — but it needs your Mac awake with the RDP window open, and you'd have to grant me access to that app. The headless screenshot path is more autonomous.

Want me to stand one up? Tell me which rendering path (Mesa software vs GPU) and I'll provision it and report back with a screenshot of the app running.
go ahead with the Mesa software path. use the elegoo-backend gcp project

content.text: The VM is up but SSH isn't answering — the OpenSSH install in the sysprep phase didn't take. Switching to a boot-time script that sets up SSH, the firewall rule, and auto-logon together.

input.command:
SP=/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/1f6398f6-3a6a-4bfb-bbfb-ebd02e54cc55/scratchpad
cat > "$SP/startup.ps1" <<'PSEOF'
$ErrorActionPreference = "Continue"
function Log($m) { Write-Host "[SETUP] $m" }

# --- 1. OpenSSH Server -------------------------------------------------
$cap = Get-WindowsCapability -Online -Name "OpenSSH.Server*"
Log "OpenSSH capability state: $($cap.State)"
if ($cap.State -ne "Installed") {
    Log "Installing OpenSSH Server..."
    Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name $cap.Name | Out-Null
    Log "Install finished, state now: $((Get-WindowsCapability -Online -Name 'OpenSSH.Server*').State)"
}
Set-Service -Name sshd -StartupType Automatic -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Start-Service sshd -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Log "sshd status: $((Get-Service sshd -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).Status)"

# PowerShell as default SSH shell
if (-not (Test-Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\OpenSSH")) { New-Item -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\OpenSSH" -Force | Out-Null }
New-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\OpenSSH" -Name DefaultShell `
  -Value "C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe" -PropertyType String -Force | Out-Null

# Firewall rule for port 22
if (-not (Get-NetFirewallRule -Name "sshd-22" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) {
    New-NetFirewallRule -Name "sshd-22" -DisplayName "OpenSSH Server (sshd)" `
      -Enabled True -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -Action Allow -LocalPort 22 | Out-Null
    Log "Created firewall rule for port 22"
}

# --- 2. Auto-logon user so a real interactive desktop exists -----------
# A GUI app launched from a remote shell lands in a session with no desktop and
# screenshots come back black. Auto-logon keeps console session 1 alive.
$user = "guitest"
if (-not (Get-LocalUser -Name $user -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) {
    Add-Type -AssemblyName System.Web
    $pw = [System.Web.Security.Membership]::GeneratePassword(24,6)
    $sec = ConvertTo-SecureString $pw -AsPlainText -Force
    New-LocalUser -Name $user -Password $sec -FullName "GUI Test" -PasswordNeverExpires -AccountNeverExpires | Out-Null
    Add-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" -Member $user | Out-Null

    $wl = "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon"
    Set-ItemProperty -Path $wl -Name "AutoAdminLogon"    -Value "1"        -Type String
    Set-ItemProperty -Path $wl -Name "DefaultUserName"   -Value $user      -Type String
    Set-ItemProperty -Path $wl -Name "DefaultPassword"   -Value $pw        -Type String
    Set-ItemProperty -Path $wl -Name "DefaultDomainName" -Value $env:COMPUTERNAME -Type String
    Log "Created auto-logon user '$user'"
}

# Never blank/lock the screen - a locked desktop screenshots as the lock screen
$wl = "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon"
Set-ItemProperty -Path $wl -Name "ScreenSaverGracePeriod" -Value "0" -Type String -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
powercfg /change monitor-timeout-ac 0
powercfg /change standby-timeout-ac 0

# --- 3. Working directory ---------------------------------------------
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "C:\guitest" -Force | Out-Null
icacls "C:\guitest" /grant "Everyone:(OI)(CI)F" /T | Out-Null
Log "Setup complete."
PSEOF
wc -l "$SP/startup.ps1"

input.command:
SP=/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/1f6398f6-3a6a-4bfb-bbfb-ebd02e54cc55/scratchpad

cat > "$SP/install-mesa-and-app.ps1" <<'PSEOF'
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$ProgressPreference = "SilentlyContinue"   # Invoke-WebRequest is ~10x faster without the progress bar
function Log($m) { Write-Host "[INSTALL] $m" }

$root = "C:\guitest"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $root -Force | Out-Null
Set-Location $root

# --- 7zr.exe: standalone extractor, Mesa ships .7z only --------------
if (-not (Test-Path "$root\7zr.exe")) {
    Log "Downloading 7zr.exe"
    Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://www.7-zip.org/a/7zr.exe" -OutFile "$root\7zr.exe"
}

# --- Mesa3D llvmpipe: software OpenGL 4.5 ----------------------------
$mesaUrl = "https://github.com/pal1000/mesa-dist-win/releases/download/26.2.0/mesa3d-26.2.0-release-msvc.7z"
if (-not (Test-Path "$root\mesa\x64\opengl32.dll")) {
    Log "Downloading Mesa3D 26.2.0 (msvc release, ~70MB)"
    Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $mesaUrl -OutFile "$root\mesa.7z"
    Log "Extracting Mesa"
    & "$root\7zr.exe" x "$root\mesa.7z" "-o$root\mesa" -y | Out-Null
}
Log "Mesa x64 contents:"
Get-ChildItem "$root\mesa\x64\*.dll" | ForEach-Object { Log "  $($_.Name)" }

# --- OrcaSlicer 2.4.2 portable (same 2.4 base as this fork) ----------
$appUrl = "https://github.com/SoftFever/OrcaSlicer/releases/download/v2.4.2/OrcaSlicer_Windows_V2.4.2_x64_portable.zip"
if (-not (Test-Path "$root\app")) {
    Log "Downloading OrcaSlicer portable (~171MB)"
    Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $appUrl -OutFile "$root\app.zip"
    Log "Extracting app"
    Expand-Archive -Path "$root\app.zip" -DestinationPath "$root\app" -Force

Stop/start is running. Meanwhile, here's where things stand — this is the substantive progress:

**The core question is answered: yes, this works.** OrcaSlicer 2.4.2 launched on a GPU-less GCE Windows VM, loaded Mesa's software OpenGL (`opengl32.dll` version 26.2.0 from `C:\guitest\app\`, confirmed in its loaded-module list), got past the OpenGL 3.2 requirement that would have killed it on stock Windows, logged `finished the gui app init`, and created its main window. I can screenshot the desktop and pull the PNG back here.

Two blockers surfaced that matter for testing JusPrin specifically:

**WebView2 was missing.** The app log said `WebView2 runtime not found; prompting user to install` and put up a modal dialog that froze startup. A clean Windows Server image has no Edge WebView2 runtime. This matters more for your fork than for stock Orca — JusPrin's UI is WebView-based, so it would hit this immediately. Installed version 152.0.4191.66.

**The display is 640×480.** The app's main window is 760×500, so it doesn't even fit. The cause is that the VM had no GCE virtual display device, so Windows fell back to its Basic Display Adapter with no EDID. `--enable-display-device` is the fix, which is the stop/start now running.

cat > /Users/kenneth/jusprin-win-vm-harness/README.md <<'EOF'
# Windows GUI test VM (GCP) — working harness

Drives a wxWidgets + OpenGL desktop app on a GPU-less Windows VM in GCP,
headlessly: launch it, screenshot it, click it, verify the result.

Verified 2026-09-07 with OrcaSlicer 2.4.2 portable.

## The VM

    instance : jusprin-win-test
    project  : elegoo-backend
    zone     : us-central1-a
    machine  : n2-standard-8, Windows Server 2022, 100GB pd-balanced
    display  : virtual display device ENABLED (required, see below)
    login    : ssh as guitest with ~/.ssh/google_compute_engine

The external IP is ephemeral and CHANGES on every stop/start. Re-read it with:

    gcloud compute instances describe jusprin-win-test --zone=us-central1-a \
      --project=elegoo-backend \
      --format="value(networkInterfaces[0].accessConfigs[0].natIP)"

then update winssh.sh / winscp.sh.

## Four things that had to be solved

1. **OpenGL.** The app hard-requires OpenGL 3.2 (src/slic3r/GUI/OpenGLManager.cpp)
   and exits below it. Stock Windows software rendering reports 1.1. Fix: drop
   Mesa's `opengl32.dll` + `libgallium_wgl.dll` (from pal1000/mesa-dist-win) next
   to the .exe. Reports OpenGL 4.2 on plain CPU.

   Mesa then auto-picks its **d3d12** backend, because the GCE virtual display
   exposes "Microsoft Basic Render Driver" as a D3D12 device — and that path
   crashed on the first frame. run-app.cmd forces the CPU rasterizer with
   `GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe` and `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1`.

   Do NOT copy the whole Mesa .7z onto the VM: Windows Defender flags the archive
   as Trojan:Win32/Suschil!rfn and deletes it. Extract the two DLLs elsewhere and
   copy just those — Defender does not object to them, so no AV exclusion is
   needed. (The archive's sha256 matches GitHub's published release digest; the
   detection is a heuristic on the bundle, which also contains Vulkan layers,
   D3D12 compilers and media-foundation encoders we don't use.)

2. **A visible desktop.** A GUI app started from an SSH shell lands in a session
   with no desktop and screenshots come back black. autologon.ps1 creates a local
   admin `guitest` and sets Winlogon AutoAdminLogon so console session 1 is always
   live. Something in the GCE image clears those values after the boot that sets
   them, so startup.ps1 re-applies them on EVERY boot.

3. **Session isolation.** Display APIs, EnumWindows and Get-Process MainWindowTitle
   only see the CALLING session's window station. Run them over SSH and they
   silently report nothing — which reads as "the app has no window" when it does.
   Everything that touches the UI goes through `Invoke-InSession` in harness.ps1,
   which registers a scheduled task with `-LogonType Interactive` so it runs in
   session 1, and writes its output to a file to be read back over SSH.

4. **Resolution.** Without a GCE virtual display device the guest falls back to
   Microsoft Basic Display Adapter with no EDID = 640x480, and the app's own
   window is 760x500. Fix (requires the instance to be STOPPED):

       gcloud compute instances stop   jusprin-win-test --zone=us-central1-a --project=elegoo-backend
       gcloud compute instances update jusprin-win-test --zone=us-central1-a --project=elegoo-backend --enable-display-device
       gcloud compute instances start  jusprin-win-test --zone=us-central1-a --project=elegoo-backend

   Then 1920x1080 is available via set-res.ps1.

## Also required by this app

Microsoft Edge WebView2 runtime is NOT present on a clean Windows Server image.
Without it the app puts up a modal "WebView2 Runtime" prompt and startup blocks
forever. Installed here as 152.0.4191.66 via the Evergreen bootstrapper:

    Invoke-WebRequest "https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/p/?LinkId=2124703" -OutFile setup.exe
    .\setup.exe /silent /install

This matters more for JusPrin than for stock Orca, since JusPrin's UI is
WebView-based.

## Files

    startup.ps1      GCE windows-startup-script-ps1: OpenSSH, port 22 firewall,
                     authorized_keys, calls autologon.ps1. Runs every boot.
    autologon.ps1    Creates guitest + sets AutoAdminLogon. Idempotent.
    harness.ps1      Invoke-InSession / Take-Screenshot. Source this first.
    screenshot.ps1   Screen capture. Must run in-session.
    probe.ps1        Lists session 1's real windows to C:\guitest\windows.txt.
    focus-app.ps1    Closes leftover task consoles, maximizes the app window.
    click.ps1        Clicks the "x,y" in C:\guitest\click.txt.
    set-res.ps1      Sets 1920x1080. Must run in-session.
    install-app.ps1  Downloads the app, places the Mesa DLLs beside the .exe.
    run-app.cmd      Launches the app with llvmpipe forced, detached.
    winssh.sh        ssh wrapper. winscp.sh: scp wrapper.

## Typical cycle

    ./winscp.sh <local.ps1> guitest@<IP>:C:/guitest/
    ./winssh.sh '. C:\guitest\harness.ps1; Invoke-InSession -TaskName "X" ...'
    ./winssh.sh '. C:\guitest\harness.ps1; Take-Screenshot'
    ./winscp.sh guitest@<IP>:C:/guitest/shot.png ./shot.png

## Known gap

There is no current JusPrin Windows binary to test. The Build all workflow's
Windows job fails at `cmake -G "Visual Studio 17 2022"` with "could not find any
instance of Visual Studio"; last green Windows build was 2026-03-04 and its
artifacts have expired. Either fix that job, or install VS Build Tools on this VM
and build from the cached OrcaSlicer_dep_win64 artifact.
EOF

content.text:
Done. Here's the summary.

**Yes — testing a GUI app on a Windows VM in GCP works, and it's now set up and proven.** OrcaSlicer 2.4.2 runs on a GPU-less Windows Server 2022 VM in the `elegoo-backend` project, rendering through Mesa's CPU-only OpenGL at 1920×1080. I can launch it, screenshot it, script clicks into it, and verify the result — the two images above show the setup wizard before and after a scripted click on "Get Started".

**The VM:** instance `jusprin-win-test`, zone `us-central1-a`, n2-standard-8, 100GB disk. SSH in as `guitest` with your existing `~/.ssh/google_compute_engine` key. Note the external IP is ephemeral and changes on every stop/start.

**Four things had to be solved, all of which fail silently rather than reporting an error:**

1. **OpenGL.** The app hard-requires 3.2 ([OpenGLManager.cpp:288](src/slic3r/GUI/OpenGLManager.cpp:288)) and stock Windows software rendering is 1.1. Dropping Mesa's `opengl32.dll` and `libgallium_wgl.dll` beside the .exe gets OpenGL 4.2 on plain CPU. But Mesa then auto-selects its Direct3D 12 backend — the GCE virtual display advertises a D3D12 device — and that path crashed on the first rendered frame. Forcing `GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe` and `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1` fixed it.

2. **Session isolation.** This one cost the most time and is worth remembering: on Windows, display APIs and window enumeration only see the calling session's window station. Run them over SSH and they return nothing — which reads exactly like "the app never created a window" when in fact it had. Everything UI-touching now runs as a scheduled task inside the logged-in desktop session.

3. **Resolution.** Without a GCE virtual display device the guest falls back to a 640×480 adapter, smaller than the app's own 760×500 window. `gcloud compute instances update --enable-display-device` (instance must be stopped) unlocks 1920×1080.

4. **WebView2 was missing.** A clean Windows Server image has no Edge WebView2 runtime; the app put up a modal prompt and startup blocked indefinitely. Installed 152.0.4191.66. **This one matters more for your fork than for stock Orca** — JusPrin's UI is WebView-based, so it would hit this immediately on any fresh Windows machine.

**On the antivirus question:** Windows Defender flagged the Mesa archive as `Trojan:Win32/Suschil!rfn` and deleted it. I didn't add an exclusion — that's a security setting and your call. Instead I verified the archive's SHA256 matches GitHub's published release digest exactly, extracted only the two DLLs I actually needed on the Mac, and copied just those. Defender doesn't object to them, so no security setting was changed at all.

**What I could not finish:** there is no current JusPrin Windows binary to test, so I proved the pipeline with stock OrcaSlicer 2.4.2 (the same 2.4 base your fork branches from). Your `Build all` CI workflow's Windows job fails at `cmake -G "Visual Studio 17 2022"` with "could not find any instance of Visual Studio". The last green Windows build was 2026-03-04 and its artifacts have expired. Two ways forward: fix that CI job, or install VS Build Tools on this VM and build there from the cached `OrcaSlicer_dep_win64` artifact, which is still available.

The harness, scripts, and a README covering all of the above are in `/Users/kenneth/jusprin-win-vm-harness/` (outside the repo, so nothing to accidentally commit).

**The VM is still running** — roughly $0.40/hour for the n2-standard-8, though I haven't verified current pricing. Want me to stop it, or leave it up while we sort out getting a JusPrin build onto it?
It's the easiest way to test, debug and fix things on Windows VM is to check out the repo and try to build it there
Good call — that also gives us a way to fix the CI break, since the same "can't find Visual Studio" failure is reproducible there. Let me gather the facts first.

cat > "$SP/build-jusprin.ps1" <<'PSEOF'
param([string]$Branch = "jusprin-newui")
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$ProgressPreference = "SilentlyContinue"
function Log($m) { Write-Host ("[BUILD {0:HH:mm:ss}] {1}" -f (Get-Date), $m) }

# This SSH session started before the toolchain set the machine PATH.
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path","Machine")

# build_release_vs.bat picks its CMake generator from `msbuild -version`, and
# Build Tools does not put MSBuild on PATH. Locate it the way CI's
# microsoft/setup-msbuild action does.
$vswhere = "${env:ProgramFiles(x86)}\Microsoft Visual Studio\Installer\vswhere.exe"
if (-not (Test-Path $vswhere)) { throw "vswhere.exe not found - VS Build Tools did not install" }
$vsPath = & $vswhere -products * -requires Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.VC.Tools.x86.x64 -property installationPath -latest
if (-not $vsPath) { throw "vswhere found no VS instance with the C++ toolset" }
Log "VS instance: $vsPath"
$msbuildDir = Join-Path $vsPath "MSBuild\Current\Bin"
if (-not (Test-Path (Join-Path $msbuildDir "MSBuild.exe"))) { throw "MSBuild.exe not under $msbuildDir" }
$env:Path = "$msbuildDir;$env:Path"
Log ("msbuild -version -> " + ((& msbuild -version) | Select-Object -Last 1))

# --- source ------------------------------------------------------------------
$repo = "C:\src\JusPrin"
if (-not (Test-Path "$repo\.git")) {
    Log "Cloning $Branch (shallow; version comes from version.inc, not git tags)"
    & git clone --depth 1 --branch $Branch --single-branch `
        "https://github.com/TheSpaghettiDetective/JusPrin.git" $repo
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "git clone failed ($LASTEXITCODE)" }
} else {
    Log "Repo already present at $repo"
}
Set-Location $repo
Log ("HEAD: " + (& git rev-parse --short HEAD) + "  branch: " + (& git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD))

# --- prebuilt deps -----------------------------------------------------------
# CI's cache path for Windows x64 is <workspace>/deps/build/OrcaSlicer_dep, and
# the artifact zip already has OrcaSlicer_dep/ at its root.
$depTarget = "$repo\deps\build"
if (-not (Test-Path "$depTarget\OrcaSlicer_dep\usr\local")) {
    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $depTarget -Force | Out-Null
    Log "Unpacking prebuilt deps into $depTarget"
    Expand-Archive -Path "C:\src\OrcaSlicer_dep_win64_20260609_vs2022.zip" -DestinationPath $depTarget -Force
}
Log ("deps present: " + (Test-Path "$depTarget\OrcaSlicer_dep\usr\local\include"))

# --- build -------------------------------------------------------------------
Log "Running build_release_vs.bat slicer"
$sw = [Diagnostics.Stopwatch]::StartNew()
& cmd /c "build_release_vs.bat slicer 2>&1"
$code = $LASTEXITCODE
$sw.Stop()
Log ("build_release_vs.bat exit={0} elapsed={1:N1} min" -f $code, $sw.Elapsed.TotalMinutes)

# --- what came out -----------------------------------------------------------
Log "--- built executables ---"
Get-ChildItem "$repo\build" -Recurse -Filter "*.exe" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
  Where-Object { $_.Length -gt 1MB } |
  Select-Object FullName, @{n="MB";e={[math]::Round($_.Length/1MB,1)}} |
  Format-Table -AutoSize | Out-String | Write-Host
exit $code

Found the real cause: `deps/Eigen/Eigen.cmake` declares `DEPENDS dep_Boost dep_GMP dep_MPFR`. So building Eigen alone forces Boost, GMP and MPFR to build first — that's why Boost downloaded. There's no shortcut here.

content.text:
Full dependency build is running now. This is a good checkpoint — here's what the VM has already told us.

**The CI failure is not a bug in the build script.** On this VM the exact same logic works: `build_release_vs.bat` runs `msbuild -version`, gets 17.14.51.32402, selects the "Visual Studio 17 2022" generator, and CMake then finds the toolchain fine — it reported `Selecting Windows SDK version 10.0.26100.0` and MSVC 19.44.35228.0, and configured successfully. So the script's Visual Studio detection is sound; what differs is the GitHub runner's Visual Studio installation. I haven't diagnosed the runner itself, so I'd stop short of saying exactly what's wrong there.

**The build got further and hit a second, separate problem.** CMake configure failed at [CMakeLists.txt:587](CMakeLists.txt:587) with `find_package(Eigen3 5.0.1 REQUIRED)` — the prebuilt dependency bundle I used contains no Eigen3 at all. To be precise about what that does and doesn't imply: I used a CI *artifact* (`OrcaSlicer_dep_win64_20260906`, which unpacks a zip named `..._20260609_...` with files dated October 2025), whereas the CI build job restores dependencies from `actions/cache` keyed on `hashFiles('deps/**')`. Those are different mechanisms, so this is a stale-artifact problem on my side, not evidence that CI's dependency cache is stale.

**Why the quick fix wasn't quick:** `deps/Eigen/Eigen.cmake` declares `DEPENDS dep_Boost dep_GMP dep_MPFR`, so building Eigen alone drags Boost, GMP and MPFR in first. Rather than patch around that, I'm doing a full dependency build so the VM ends up with a bundle that actually matches the source. Expect 1–3 hours on 8 vCPUs.

**One thing you should know:** your local branch is 5 commits ahead of `origin/jusprin-newui` (`493344b59a` locally vs `1db32fbe` on the remote), including "Align the header print dropdown with menu conventions". The VM cloned from GitHub, so it's building without your unpushed work. When the build succeeds I can transfer those commits with a git bundle over SSH — no pushing required — unless you'd rather push them.

content.text:
Rebuild is running. Here's what the last round found — three failures, and the diagnosis matters because two were caused by how I ran things, not by the code.

**libpng (a real setup gap).** The build died with `Cannot open include file: 'pngprefix.h'`. The project passes `-DPNG_PREFIX=prusaslicer_` in [deps/PNG/PNG.cmake](deps/PNG/PNG.cmake), which makes libpng generate that header using an awk script. Its CMakeCache recorded `AWK:FILEPATH=AWK-NOTFOUND`. Git for Windows ships `awk.exe` in `usr\bin`, but when I set up the toolchain I only added Git's `cmd` directory to PATH. Fixed by adding `C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin`.

**OpenSSL (my fault).** It failed with `fatal error C1033: cannot open program database 'ossl_static.pdb'` — the signature of two compilers writing the same debug database at once. That traces to the window where two builds briefly ran in the same directory, before I moved to the scheduled task. Wiped and rebuilding.

**Boost (also my fault).** OpenVDB failed because `boost_bind-config-version.cmake` was 2360 bytes of non-printable data. Its timestamp is 14:12:00, which is when the machine was force-stopped for the resize — the file was allocated but never flushed. I removed Boost's install stamp and the installed `boost_*` CMake configs so they get rewritten.

Net: 19 of 25 dependencies are good, Eigen is now installed at the path CMake wanted, and the three broken ones are rebuilding. I'll report when it finishes.

cat > "$DEST/BUILDING.md" <<'EOF'
# Building JusPrin from source on the Windows VM

Verified 2026-09-07: full build from a clean VM, then run and screenshotted.
Total ~1h10m of machine time on n2-standard-16 (16 vCPU, 64 GB).

    deps build   22.7 min   (all 24 applicable deps from source)
    slicer build 23.0 min
    output       C:\src\JusPrin\build\src\Release\orca-slicer.exe (261 KB launcher)
                 + OrcaSlicer.dll (122.7 MB — the actual application)

## Order of operations

1. `install-buildtools.ps1` — CMake 4.3.5 (CI pins ~4.3.0), Ninja, Git for
   Windows, Strawberry Perl, and VS 2022 Build Tools with the VCTools workload.
2. Clone the repo (public, no credentials needed). Shallow is fine: the version
   comes from `version.inc`, not git tags.
3. `build-deps-full.ps1` — builds all deps. **Do not use the CI dependency
   artifact**; see below.
4. `build-slicer.ps1` — runs `build_release_vs.bat slicer`.
5. Put Mesa where the app looks for it, then `run-jusprin.cmd`.

## Things that will bite you

**Run long builds as a SCHEDULED TASK, not over SSH.** Windows OpenSSH kills the
whole process tree when the session ends, so a build started from an SSH command
(even detached with Start-Process) dies on disconnect. Register it instead:

    New-ScheduledTaskPrincipal -UserId "SYSTEM" -LogonType ServiceAccount -RunLevel Highest

Two builds racing in one directory corrupt each other — OpenSSL failed with
`C1033: cannot open program database ossl_static.pdb` when that happened here.

**awk must be on PATH.** `deps/PNG/PNG.cmake` passes `-DPNG_PREFIX=prusaslicer_`,
so libpng generates `pngprefix.h` with an awk script. Without awk you get
`AWK-NOTFOUND` in the PNG CMakeCache and then `C1083: Cannot open include file:
'pngprefix.h'`. Git for Windows ships awk — add `C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin`
to PATH, not just `C:\Program Files\Git\cmd`.

**Set `CMAKE_POLICY_VERSION_MINIMUM=3.5`.** Several bundled CMakeLists still
declare pre-3.5 minimums, which CMake 4.x rejects outright.

**The CI dependency artifact is unusable.** `OrcaSlicer_dep_win64_20260906`

**Done — JusPrin now builds from source on the Windows VM and the built binary runs.** The screenshot above is our code: the Agent panel, "Set up the agent", and the chat composer are JusPrin's UI, not stock OrcaSlicer.

**Timings** on the resized VM (16 vCPU, 64 GB): dependencies 22.7 minutes, slicer 23.0 minutes. Output is `C:\src\JusPrin\build\src\Release\orca-slicer.exe` (a 261 KB launcher) plus `OrcaSlicer.dll` at 122.7 MB, which is the actual application.

**The CI question is answered.** The Windows CI job fails at `cmake -G "Visual Studio 17 2022"` with "could not find any instance of Visual Studio". That is **not** a bug in `build_release_vs.bat`. On the VM the same script read `msbuild -version` as 17.14.51.32402, selected the identical generator, and configured fine — because there's a properly registered Visual Studio Build Tools instance. The GitHub runner's environment is what's broken.

**Five problems along the way, and two were mine:**

1. **The CI dependency artifact is unusable.** `OrcaSlicer_dep_win64_20260906` contains a bundle built 2025-10-17, predating `deps/Eigen`. The source needs Eigen 5.0.1, so configure failed. Dependencies must be built from source.

2. **awk wasn't on PATH.** `deps/PNG/PNG.cmake` passes `-DPNG_PREFIX=prusaslicer_`, so libpng generates `pngprefix.h` via awk. Its CMakeCache recorded `AWK-NOTFOUND`, and the visible symptom was `C1083: Cannot open include file: 'pngprefix.h'` — an error far from its cause. Git for Windows ships awk in `usr\bin`; I'd only added `cmd`.

3. **Two builds collided (my fault).** OpenSSL failed with `C1033: cannot open program database` because two compilers wrote one PDB. Root cause: Windows OpenSSH kills the process tree on disconnect, so my builds kept dying and I restarted one on top of another. Fixed by running builds as a scheduled task under SYSTEM, which I verified survives disconnects.

4. **Hard-stopping the VM for the resize corrupted the build (my fault).** 622 of 22,011 installed files came back as NUL bytes, surfacing as bogus syntax errors inside Boost headers. A clean rebuild fixed it; the download cache meant no re-downloading.

5. **Qhull is absent by design** — `deps/CMakeLists.txt` comments it out under `if (MSVC)`, so 24 dependencies is complete on Windows.

**One genuinely useful discovery:** the app already supports software rendering on Windows natively. [src/OrcaSlicer_app_msvc.cpp:268](src/OrcaSlicer_app_msvc.cpp:268) loads `<exe dir>\mesa\opengl32.dll` when system OpenGL is below 2.0, and it printed "MESA OpenGL library was loaded successfully". That's cleaner than the DLL-drop I used on the stock build earlier.

Scripts and two write-ups (`README.md` for VM setup, `BUILDING.md` for the build) are in `/Users/kenneth/jusprin-win-vm-harness/`.

**Two things to note.** The VM built commit `1db32fbe` from origin, but your local branch is **5 commits ahead and unpushed** — so this binary doesn't include your latest header-dropdown work. I can transfer those via a git bundle without pushing, if you want to test them. And the VM is still running at 16 vCPUs, which costs roughly twice the 8-vCPU rate; say the word and I'll stop it or size it back down.

Found it precisely. Both failures are the same pattern, at [HeaderControls.cpp:549](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Shell/HeaderControls.cpp:549) and [:564](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Shell/HeaderControls.cpp:564): a `wxWeakRef<wxWindow>(this)` init-capture inside a **nested** lambda. MSVC binds that `this` to the enclosing closure object instead of the `HeaderMenu`, so it tries to build a `wxWeakRef<wxWindow>` from a lambda pointer. Clang accepts it, MSVC doesn't.

Let me verify a fix on the VM without touching your repo.

# MSVC binds `this` inside a NESTED lambda's init-capture to the enclosing
# closure object, not the enclosing class, so wxWeakRef<wxWindow>(this) tries to

$o1 = "                CallAfter([self=wxWeakRef<wxWindow>(this),action] { if (self) action(); });"

content.text:
Done. **Your latest branch does not compile on Windows as pushed — I found the bug, verified a one-line fix, and then tested the app.**

**The build break.** `fbe5963b` fails with 37 MSVC errors, all from two lines in [HeaderControls.cpp:549](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Shell/HeaderControls.cpp:549) and [:564](src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Shell/HeaderControls.cpp:564):

```
error C2149: 'wxWeakRef<wxWindow>::Assign::wxAssert_10::
  Tracked_class_should_inherit_from_wxTrackable': named bit field cannot have zero width
  with [ TDerived=const Slic3r::GUI::JusPrin::HeaderMenu::build::<lambda_9390d924...> ]
```

Both are `CallAfter([self=wxWeakRef<wxWindow>(this),...])` written **inside another lambda**. MSVC binds that `this` to the enclosing closure object rather than the `HeaderMenu`, so it tries to build a `wxWeakRef<wxWindow>` from a lambda pointer. Clang resolves it to the class, which is why macOS never showed it. Naming the object first fixes it:

```cpp
auto* menu = this;
CallAfter([self=wxWeakRef<wxWindow>(menu),action] { if (self) action(); });
```

With that applied on the VM only — I did **not** touch your repo — the build is clean, exit 0 in 4 minutes. The patch is saved at `/Users/kenneth/jusprin-win-vm-harness/msvc-nested-lambda-this.patch` for you to apply and commit as you see fit.

**Then I tested the actual app.** I ran it, stepped through the setup wizard (region → Klipper printer → filaments → stealth mode → finish), and exercised the new chips:

- The header now shows **two separate chips** — "Generic Klipper Printer · 0.4" and "Teal PLA" — matching the printer-and-spool-chip commit.

=== fork-stewardship.md ===
# Fork stewardship

**Status:** Required discipline for every change to an upstream-owned file on `jusprin-newui`.

JusPrin is a long-lived fork. Every line it changes in an OrcaSlicer-owned file is a line it re-resolves at every rebase, forever, by a person who was not there when the line was written. The rules below exist to keep that permanent cost small and, where it cannot be small, to keep it visible.

One question generates all of them: **after this change, what does the fork own?**

- Owning *product policy* is safe. It is ours, upstream will never write it, and it lives in our files.
- Owning a *small neutral seam* is acceptable. It is the kind of thing upstream might plausibly have written itself, so it survives refactors and could be contributed back.
- Owning *upstream's behavior* is the expensive kind. It commits us to re-deriving upstream's intent forever, and the day we take ownership is usually the day the behavior quietly diverges.

Two mechanical facts drive everything else. Git merges text, not meaning: it conflicts when two sides touch the same or adjacent lines, and it stays silent when they touch different lines even if the result is nonsense. And a conflict is a *stop* — a human is forced to look — while silent divergence is unbounded and invisible. Conflicts are therefore not the enemy. Unnoticed drift is, and conflicts that resolve wrongly are.

## The ten principles

### 1. Conflict probability is about where you write, not how much

**Rule.** Place fork edits where upstream rarely writes, and keep the number of distinct sites low.

**Mechanism.** Risk is roughly *how often upstream edits this region* times *how much of the region you occupy*, summed over every place you touched. Each site is an independent draw. New files have probability zero, so their size is free; one line inside a function upstream is actively reworking is expensive.

**The test.** How many separate places does this change touch, and how busy is each one? Would one seam deliver the same capability?

**Violation.** Delivering a single capability through a dozen scattered notification lines across several upstream files, when one funnel that every path already passes through would have carried them.

### 2. A clean merge is not a safe merge

**Rule.** Prefer edits that are locally correct over edits that participate in upstream's control flow.

**Mechanism.** Git merges text. If your edit's correctness depends on the code around it — an ordering, a guard, an early return, an invariant nobody wrote down — upstream can restructure the surroundings, the merge succeeds, and your edit now runs under assumptions that no longer hold, with no signal at all.

**The test.** If upstream restructures the code around this hunk, do I get a conflict or silence? If silence, would any test catch it?

**Violation.** Moving a member out of a constructor's initializer list because a callback can fire mid-construction. Nothing in upstream's code records that invariant, so a future cleanup restores the old form with no conflict and no error.

### 3. Add to upstream's code; do not revise it

**Rule.** Append, insert, and call. Do not rewrite upstream functions or change their signatures.

**Mechanism.** An additive hook fails gracefully: when it conflicts, the resolution is "keep both," and anyone can do that correctly. A rewritten function fails badly: every future upstream change to it is a conflict whose resolution requires re-deriving two intents at once, in code no longer shared with upstream. Rewriting subtle logic also tends to change it, and you find out later.

**The test.** Does upstream's line survive my change? If I deleted or replaced one, why could I not have added next to it?

**Violation.** Replacing OrcaSlicer's undo and redo implementations with fork-owned equivalents in order to learn whether the history position moved. Re-expressing the vendor-specific snapshot walk silently dropped one of its branches. An additive helper that reports the result, leaving upstream's functions untouched, would have answered the same question.

### 4. Own the policy; borrow the mechanism

**Rule.** No product name, color, dimension, or product-specific decision in an upstream-owned file. Upstream files may gain small neutral capabilities; the policy that uses them lives in fork-owned code.

**Mechanism.** Product specifics in upstream files are permanent divergence: they can never be upstreamed and never dropped, so they must be re-resolved forever. A neutral capability — a flag, a getter/setter pair, an event — reads like something upstream could have written, which is exactly why it survives refactors.

**The test.** Would this addition look reasonable in an upstream pull request, with no explanation of our product?

**Violation.** A product-named enum value inside a rendering class, or product decisions embedded in an upstream mouse handler. The fix is a neutral options struct plus a fork-owned controller that applies our policy.

### 5. One seam beats many touch points

**Rule.** Find the single place every path already passes through, and put the fork's line there.

**Mechanism.** Each touch point is an independent conflict draw and an independent thing a future resolver must understand. Collapsing many small recurring costs into one is worth some indirection.

**The test.** Do all the paths I am hooking already converge somewhere downstream? Is there one function that runs exactly when the thing I care about has happened?

**Violation.** Publishing a history-changed event from undo, from redo, and from both history-navigation entry points, when all four funnel through a single update function that runs only on a successful move.

### 6. One shared implementation is worth a guaranteed conflict

**Rule.** When the alternative is two copies of the same behavior, keep the shared path and accept that it will conflict.

content.text:
Fixed and verified. The change sits uncommitted in your working tree (and identically on the VM — same SHA256).

**The bug.** `build_release_vs.bat` never checked a single exit code. It ran cmake configure, cmake build, gettext and install in sequence, then fell into `:done`, whose last statement is `echo Build completed in ...`. A batch script exits with the status of its last command, and `echo` always succeeds — so the script returned 0 no matter what failed.

**The fix** is 21 added lines, nothing modified or deleted. Eleven `if errorlevel 1 goto :failed` guards after each fallible step, an explicit `exit /b 0` at the end of `:done`, and a `:failed` handler:

```bat
:failed
set "_rc=%ERRORLEVEL%"
if "%_rc%"=="0" set "_rc=1"
echo.
echo Build FAILED with exit code %_rc%
exit /b %_rc%
```

`ERRORLEVEL` is captured into `_rc` before anything else runs, because `echo` would reset it. I used `if errorlevel 1` rather than `if %ERRORLEVEL% neq 0` because the cmake calls sit inside parenthesized `if/else` blocks, where `%ERRORLEVEL%` expands at parse time and would read a stale value.

Per the fork-stewardship rules for upstream-owned files, every guard is a *new line beside* an upstream command rather than a modification of it, so upstream's lines survive byte-identical and a future rebase conflict resolves as "keep both".

**Three tests, all on the VM:**

1. **Reproduced first, per the bug-fix policy.** I held an exclusive handle on `OrcaSlicer.dll` to force `LNK1104`, deliberately rather than by accident. Before the fix: LNK1104 twice, **exit code 0**. After: same failure, **exit code 1**.
